A playwright and performer whose indelible, subversive and audaciously funny What The Constitution Means To Me opens tonight on Broadway at the Theatre, Schreck has carried a particular true-life story within her for 30-odd years, and she springs it on us when we need it most.
It’s a play of ideas for which people are not just hungry but starved.

It’s also exhilarating because it really places Schreck in a different kind of legacy.

It is enormously effective, offering something crucial to all political shows, which is hope for the future.
Schreck has fashioned a theatrical work of such personalized and pointed commentary that it manages to be both deeply intimate and powerfully political.
Ultimately it poses more questions — serious questions — than it answers.

Schreck makes a compelling argument that no governing document will ever be a panacea for society's ills, and that we will always have to depend on the good faith (or contend with the lack thereof) of the people charged with interpreting that document.

cn.t: Critics hail Schreck's ingeniously structured civics lesson as timely, moving, and essential theater that's both deeply personal and politically urgent. Most praise its blend of autobiography and constitutional analysis, though a few find it more lecture than drama.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's smallest houses (597 seats) and one of its newest, built in 2015 as Second Stage's permanent home. The intimate scale means excellent sightlines from nearly every seat, though the modern design prioritizes function over grandeur.
